item.title: SIGNN++: Robust Graph Neural Star Identification on Earth
item.description: arXiv:2610.30186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SIGNN++, a learning-based star identification (SID) framework for celestial navigation in GNSS-denied nighttime environments. Although researchers have developed learning-based SID methods to improve robustness to observation noise, prior evaluations have focused mainly on synthetic or non-terrestrial environments, leaving their reliability under real terrestrial conditions unclear. To address these limitations, SIGNN++ extends SIGNN, a graph neural network-based SID method, with three components: a more realistic noise model for training data, Fourier Transform (FT) of angular-distance edge features, and RANSAC-based Perspective Star Alignment for identification and attitude refinement. The results show that SIGNN++ is more robust to terrestrial observation disturbances and achieves higher star identification accuracy and solved rates than the original SIGNN and publicly available SID baselines, while maintaining comparable attitude accuracy and practical computation time for continuous operation. The implementation code of SIGNN++ and datasets will be available at https://signnpp.github.io/signnpp/.
item.dc:creator: Jeongbin Sohn, Jina Lee, Max Yen, Dowan Gwon, Jeahn Han, Floyd Hepburn-Dickins, Brian Coltin, Ryan Soussan, Pyojin Kim

item.title: Astro2Method: Benchmarking LLMs on Machine Learning Method Selection in Astronomy
item.description: arXiv:2610.30282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in astronomy, but choosing a suitable method for a scientific problem often requires expertise in both astronomy and ML. Large language models (LLMs) could help astronomers make such choices, yet this ability remains underexplored in existing benchmarks. We introduce Astro2Method, a benchmark of 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers (2024/01-2026/06), based on clear performance differences and complete (Easy) or partial (Hard) explanations from the authors. Across five LLMs, direct prompting achieves 87.50-92.55% accuracy on Easy questions but only 58.87-64.52% on Hard. Using historical papers, neither retrieval-augmented generation nor most agent methods with additional reasoning or retrieval (including ReAct, Self-Ask, and CRITIC) bring consistent improvement. Agents required to search the web improve accuracy mainly when they find the papers the questions are based on, with no consistent improvement otherwise. Providing the source paper's pipeline description with method names masked improves Hard accuracy, matching or exceeding web search. Together, these results suggest that relevant experimental information helps distinguish ML methods, but inferring it from related studies and domain knowledge remains challenging for LLMs in astronomy.
item.dc:creator: Xingzhong Fan, Hangfeng He, Fatemeh Nargesian

item.title: A Technical Reanalysis of the Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release Experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.30368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The 1976 Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release (CAPyR) experiment tested whether carbon from $^{14}$CO$_2$ and $^{14}$CO entered Martian soil during a 120-hour incubation in a form retained during a 120 $^\circ$C purge but released by pyrolysis at 635 $^\circ$C. Untrapped radioactivity was measured as Peak 1; material retained in an organic vapor trap was oxidized and measured as Peak 2. Net Peak 2 was intended to represent synthesized reduced organic carbon. Seven of nine usable incubations at Chryse and Utopia Planitia yielded significant net Peak 2 signals, including the dark U1 run. An underreported Viking Lander 2 gas leak introduces uncertainty into U1-U3. The C1 signal corresponds to approximately 10 or 30 pmol of carbon, assuming derivation entirely from CO or CO$_2$, respectively. We reassess these results in light of the possible presence of perchlorate salts in Viking soils. Oxidation of fixed organic radiocarbon during pyrolysis could have shifted label from Peak 2 to Peak 1, a perchlorate-specific effect not considered in previous CAPyR analyses. Hubbard's (1979) mineral-substrate experiments produced abiotic Peak 2 signals without reproducing the heat sensitivity. No demonstrated abiotic mechanism has reproduced all CAPyR observations under Mars-relevant conditions. The observations remain consistent with a biological carbon-assimilation system whose relevant activity survives C5's 120 $^\circ$C/90 $^\circ$C pretreatment but is strongly impaired by C2's 175 $^\circ$C pretreatment. Together with the Labeled Release experiment, CAPyR suggests oxidative and reductive chemistry in separate aliquots from common Martian soil acquisitions. Metabolically active life combines these processes; a quantitative abiotic explanation of their combined heat-labile response patterns remains to be demonstrated.
item.dc:creator: Jan Spacek, Clay A. Abraham, Steven A. Benner

item.title: The Pandora SmallSat: post-launch operations and mission update
item.description: arXiv:2610.30372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA flight project designed to study the atmospheres of exoplanets. Transmission spectroscopy of transiting exoplanets provides our best opportunity to identify the makeup of planetary atmospheres in the coming decade, and is a key science driver for HST and JWST. Stellar photospheric inhomogeneity due to star spots, however, has been shown to contaminate the observed spectra in these high-precision measurements. Pandora will address the problem of stellar contamination by collecting long-duration photometric observations sampled over a stellar rotation period with a visible-light channel and simultaneous spectra with a near-IR channel. These simultaneous multiwavelength observations will constrain star spot covering fractions of exoplanet host stars, enabling star and planet signals to be disentangled in transmission spectra to then reliably determine exoplanet atmosphere compositions. Pandora will observe exoplanets with sizes ranging from Earth-size to Jupiter-size and host stars spanning mid-K to late-M spectral types. Pandora was selected in early 2021 as part of NASA's inaugural Astrophysics Pioneers Program. Herein, we present an overview of the mission, including the science objectives, operations, the observatory, science planning, and upcoming milestones as we prepare for launch readiness in 2025.

item.title: Photometric classification and out-of-taxonomy detection of ZTF transients with FLARE
item.description: arXiv:2610.30656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photometric classifiers decide which of the million nightly alerts of time-domain surveys receive one of the few thousand spectra taken each year, and they are the first place where a transient outside the trained classes can be noticed. We present flare, the photometric classification and anomaly-detection module of AppleCiDEr, evaluated on 10 497 spectroscopically confirmed ZTF transients in six classes and 53 objects from families outside the taxonomy. Catalogue context raises the macro F1 score, with the largest gains where the defining information is absent from the light curve. Blind detection recovers few out-of-taxonomy objects at a 1% false-alarm rate, while a simulated review loop recovers 83% of them after inspecting 15% of the stream. The first confirmations of a new family are most useful in the feature space: with the same eleven labels, a head on the frozen features detects 68% of the tidal disruption events hidden from the training against 57% for a combiner over the anomaly scores, and retraining with them as a new class reaches 85%. The module runs in production on Fritz, the ZTF instance of SkyPortal, and its alarm is reported as a false-alarm rate per unit time on the stream, calibrated on the photometry that the service receives

item.title: Astrometric detection of rocky exoplanets from inexpensive space platforms
item.description: arXiv:2610.30806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The detection of orbiting exoplanets by way of astrometric monitoring of the host star to reveal gravitationally induced reflex motion requires extreme precision and measurement stability when targeting Earth-mass objects. Despite this, astrometry is widely regarded as the most promising avenue for the most desired of all targets: true Earth analogue systems in the solar neighbourhood. Formerly thought to require flagship class investment, recently several smaller concepts such as the TOLIMAN and SHERA missions have shown that detections are possible, at least in principle, from more modest space platforms. A key enabling feature is that these missions exploit narrow-angle astrometry. Observing only multiple star systems where the target provides its own astrometric reference greatly alleviates the challenges confronted by traditional astrometry with its reliance on distant, faint field stars. This principle underlies the TOLIMAN mission, for which progress and status is reported. However, only a tiny handful of nearby star systems are suited to such a TOLIMAN-like architecture. This paper discusses speculative optical concepts featuring ultra-stable telescopes of modest (<0.5m) aperture designed for astrometric monitoring of isolated single stars at the micro-arcsecond scales required for the discovery of Earth mass objects orbiting sun-like stars in temperate orbits. In simulation, highly sought-after neighbourhood systems such as Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti can be exhaustively searched for rocky planets with dedicated observing campaigns spanning several years, all from relatively inexpensive orbital platforms.

item.title: Science-driven design and performance evaluation of a Silicon Laue Component lens for hard X-ray polarimetry
item.description: arXiv:2610.31287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Focusing hard X-rays above 80 keV is challenging for grazing-incidence optics. Laue lenses offer an alternative based on crystal diffraction. We assess a lens based on Silicon Laue Components (SiLCs), consisting of stacked silicon plates, for polarimetry of accreting stellar-mass black holes and strongly magnetized neutron stars in the 80-200 keV band. We derive effective-area requirements from the minimum detectable polarization at 99% confidence (MDP99) for an XL-Calibur-inspired polarimeter observing a 100-mCrab source for 100 ks. We evaluate an 18-m-focal-length lens combining Si(220) and Si(111) reflections, with a 63 arcsec diffraction bandpass and a 90% optical filling factor, using on-axis ray tracing of a perfectly aligned lens with uniform crystal curvatures. An MDP99 of 5% requires mean effective areas of approximately 260, 400, and 740 cm^2 in the 80-100, 100-130, and 130-200 keV bands, respectively. The lens spans radii of 356-1453 mm and continuously covers 80-200 keV. Its effective area reaches approximately 375 cm^2 near the low-energy boundary and falls to approximately 200 cm^2 at 180 keV. The focal-plane diameters enclosing 50% and 90% of the focused signal are 5.4 mm (62 arcsec) and 9.8 mm (112 arcsec). Mean effective areas of approximately 320, 250, and 220 cm^2 give reference MDP99 values of approximately 4.5%, 6.4%, and 9.5% in the three bands. The design reaches few-percent polarimetric sensitivity below 100 keV but does not maintain a 5% MDP99 across 80-200 keV under the adopted detector assumptions. It remains relevant for more strongly polarized hard components and provides a reference for end-to-end optimization of the optics, detector response, and background.
item.dc:creator: L. Abalo, N. M. Barri\`ere, M. W. Beijersbergen

item.title: Simulation-based inference of profile evolution for high-precision pulsar timing
item.description: arXiv:2610.31450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pulsars are exceptional cosmic laboratories, the most stable of which rival atomic clocks. Nearly all of that precision rests on one observable, the average pulse profile unique to each pulsar and stable over decades. These profiles change shape systematically with observing frequency, reflecting the physics of the emitting pulsar beam, but if left unmodelled, it can bias the arrival-time measurements, undermining precision timing. Profile-domain timing has been proposed to address this effect, but current implementations use stochastic sampling, which is computationally prohibitive and has limited the application in large-scale analyses. Here, we present a simulation-based inference approach to profile-domain timing, using a normalising flow conditioned on a convolutional embedding of the frequency-phase portrait. From a single portrait, it returns joint posteriors on dispersion measures, arrival times, and the parameters governing profile evolution instantaneously, with uncertainties verified against known inputs following an initial training run. The value of a likelihood-free approach is that the simulator becomes the interface to pulsar properties. Fundamental properties like non-Gaussian noise, pulsar self-noise, jitter, scattering, and profile change can be inferred by simulating them rather than by deriving a new likelihood for each, opening a promising pathway to include machine learning methods into pulsar timing workflows.
item.dc:creator: Sai C. Susarla, Gregory Ashton, A. Parthasarathy, K. De Man, J. P. W. Verbiest

item.title: A Generalized Framework for Rapid Polarization Response Generation in Wide Field-of-View Compton Polarimeters
item.description: arXiv:2610.31559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polarimetry is the most direct probe of the unsettled radiation mechanism and magnetic field structure of gamma-ray burst (GRB) prompt emission at the energies where it peaks, tens of keV to about 1 MeV. Compton polarimeters use the azimuthal scattering angle distribution (ASAD), a 180 degree modulation on axis. GRB measurements have largely relied on the on-axis modulation factor $\mu_{100}$. For a wide field-of-view planar polarimeter, GRBs arrive off axis, where the Klein-Nishina projection adds harmonics to the ASAD. Muleri (2014) described this projection and evaluated it in a low-energy expansion for X-rays. We evaluate it numerically without approximation over the whole prompt-emission energy band for any incidence and polarization angles, quantify the off-axis harmonics a single modulation factor cannot capture, and verify the model against GEANT4 simulations of an ideal polarimeter. We also include the effect of the detection threshold on the ASAD. With POLAR as the case study, we present two modes that build the full polarization response with at least 95 percent fewer Monte Carlo simulations. Mode 1 takes only the unpolarized simulation per energy and recovers the polarization measured with POLAR's full GEANT4 responses for all but the brightest GRBs, where it underestimates the polarization degree. Mode 2 adds two polarized simulations per energy at distinct angles and reproduces the simulated ASADs to their statistical noise and the polarization of every GRB tested. Both modes are released as open-source software for any planar Compton polarimeter.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Gamal Zaid, Merlin Kole, Mark McConnell, Fabio Muleri, Hancheng Li

item.title: Confirming candidate self-lensing binary detections with radial velocity measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.30203v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Compact objects in approximately edge-on binary orbits with stars are able to produce a self-lensing effect, amplifying light from their companion once per orbit. To date, five white dwarf self-lensing systems are known, while none are known containing black holes or neutron stars. Discovery of such systems is a potential method of finding quiescent black holes and neutron stars, most of which will be pristine and unchanged from their formation. Photometric detections can suffer from degeneracies in the lens mass and orbital parameters when the amplification and crossing time are not well constrained, while photometric searches produce too many false positives to allow radial velocity investigation of every candidate. Therefore we investigate the minimal radial velocity (RV) observational requirements to characterise such systems by simulating detectable self-lensing light curves, using those light curves to generate targeted RV observations, and fitting RV jointly with photometry. We evaluate the median relative error in the recovered lens mass and orbital period, alongside compact-object class recovery. We find that adding RV measurements substantially reduces parameter error, with compact-object class generally easier to determine than the exact lens mass. Parameter accuracy is driven mainly by number of RV observations, with RV precision playing a weaker role except for the shortest-period systems, with even a small number of RV measurements resulting in substantial improvement in accuracy. These results suggest that multi-stage RV follow-up, starting with a small number of observations of many candidates, can efficiently classify self-lensing candidates and identify high-priority systems for further investigation.
item.dc:creator: Adam McMaster, Madeline-Mai Ward, Hugh J. Dickinson, Matthew J. Middleton, D. J. Dixon, Adam Ingram, N. Castro Segura, Simon Vaughan, Grzegorz Wiktorowicz

item.title: Analog Electronic Computation of Stellar Structure: Polytropic Benchmarks, Circuit Scaling, and Error-Controlled Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.30230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present an electronic analog-computing framework for static stellar-structure equations and verify it using polytropic Lane-Emden benchmarks with known or high-accuracy reference solutions. Starting from an exploratory operational-amplifier and multiplier circuit, we identify sign, coefficient, central-regularity, and signal-conditioning problems that complicate direct electronic implementation. We develop dimensionless first-order formulations, derive regular finite-radius initial conditions, and construct voltage-scaled analog architectures with controlled signal headroom. The principal formulation uses a positive derivative state and reproduces the surface locations and dimensionless mass coefficients of the n = 0, 1, and 3 polytropes at the ideal scaled-voltage level. A common circuit architecture accommodates all three benchmarks, while the nonlinear n = 3 case demonstrates how voltage scaling and computation-speed adjustments can preserve the governing equations. Sensitivity analysis and Monte Carlo simulations quantify the propagation of calibration uncertainties into stellar observables. A separate regularized n = 1 circuit, implemented using AD734 and OPAx197 vendor macromodels, passes all 67 deterministic certification cases and three independently seeded Monte Carlo populations of 1000 cases each. All cases satisfy the predefined first-zero error tolerance of 0.020, with no saturation or convergence failures. A stricter 0.1% accuracy threshold is reported for characterization but is not used as the certification criterion. We also demonstrate a dimensionless four-state radiative extension beyond polytropic models. The results establish a reproducible framework for analog computation of stellar-structure benchmarks while explicitly distinguishing ideal calculations, vendor-macromodel verification, and future physical-hardware validation.
item.dc:creator: Zuhoor Elahi, Wafa Gull, Christopher Sirola

item.title: OGLE-2012-BLG-0563: Relative Proper Motion Constraint from Keck Follow-up finds the correct Lens
item.description: arXiv:2610.30310v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present Keck/NIRC2 adaptive optics imaging results of planetary microlensing event OGLE-2012-BLG-0563. We find that the OGLE-2012-BLG-0563L planetary system consists of a 1.12 +/- 0.09 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting a 0.81 +/- 0.04 solar-mass host star at a distance of 5.49 +/- 0.56 kpc from the Sun. This event has a lens-source separation of 23.28 +/- 0.48 mas, which is the smallest lens-source separation measured to date with Keck AO data. We find that the incorrect solution - which identifies the Northeast (NE) star as the source star - is favored if one only considers the discovery paper, the Fukui et al. (2015) solution, or an unconstrained model. However, by performing an image-constrained light curve model fit using the relative proper motion direction constraint from the Keck follow-up data, we demonstrate that the correct solution identifies the NE star as the lens star. The discrepancy in the unconstrained models is driven by systematics in the FTS and MOA B & C data, alongside the impact of the relative proper motion direction constraints. This outcome offers two important lessons for future Roman data analysis: (1) thoroughly verify systematics across all passbands and identify the precise origin of chi-squared differences, and (2) utilize image-constrained light curve modeling incorporating relative proper motion direction constraints to identify the correct lens.

item.title: From Venus to the Parking Lot: A Flexible Stellar Interferometry Experiment
item.description: arXiv:2610.30669v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We describe a simple extension of our earlier Venus interferometry demonstration that can be performed indoors or outdoors, independent of planetary visibility or atmospheric seeing. A small flashlight is placed 15-50 meters away from a telescope and covered with a circular aperture mask (hole diameter 2-6~mm). A small telescope fitted with an opaque mask bearing two 2~mm holes, spaced between 5 and 20~mm apart, is then used to observe interference fringes from this artificial extended source. By varying the hole separation and observing the fringes students can estimate the angular diameter of the source and verify their result directly by simple geometry, a check not possible with astronomical targets. The experiment requires no telescope tracking, no dark skies, and no special equipment beyond materials described in the original paper. It serves equally well as a pre-lab to build intuition before observing Venus, a standalone indoor daytime or outdoor nighttime activity, or a quantitative test of the interferometric method itself.
item.dc:creator: Eric J. Friedman, Michelle Goman

item.title: Natural Chlorine Enhances Antineutrino Detection in the Deep Ocean
item.description: arXiv:2610.30754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-volume neutrino telescopes such as IceCube and KM3NeT exploit natural ice or water as detection media, but their sparse instrumentation makes MeV neutrino interactions difficult to identify individually. We show that chlorine naturally abundant in seawater provides an intrinsic neutron-capture target that enables efficient tagging of electron antineutrinos through inverse beta decay. In contrast to the 2.2 MeV $\gamma$-ray from neutron capture on hydrogen, capture on chlorine produces an $\sim$8.6 MeV $\gamma$-ray cascade on a shorter time scale, yielding a distinctive delayed-coincidence signature. Using measured seawater properties at the TRIDENT site and a detector-level simulation, we find that chlorine-assisted tagging can extend the core-collapse supernova 5$\sigma$ discovery reach from $\sim$50 to over 100 kpc. We validate the underlying detection principle with a salted-water experiment at the China Jinping Underground Laboratory, observing correlated neutron-capture signatures under suppressed cosmic muon background conditions. Natural seawater thus transforms the deep ocean into an intrinsically enhanced antineutrino detection medium, opening new opportunities for MeV neutrino astronomy and distributed measurements of reactor and geophysical antineutrinos.
item.dc:creator: Ruike Cao, Iwan Morton-Blake, Donglian Xu, Qichao Chang, Shuhua Hao, Jingtao Huang, Weilun Huang, Yifan Jiang, Shasha Liu, Hualin Mei, Hengbin Shao, Yingwei Wang, Peilian Wu, Xin Xiang, Fuyudi Zhang, Haoyan Zhang, Zhaozhi Zhang, Tailin Zhu, Yiwei Zhu

item.title: Lomb-Scargle Recovery of Periodic Binary Signals across Black Hole Mass and Cadence
item.description: arXiv:2610.30772v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Searches for periodic supermassive black hole binaries in quasar light curves rely on recovery fractions, the share of injected signals detected, which forecasts use as detection efficiencies. Lin, Charisi, & Haiman (2026) measured them for the Lomb-Scargle periodogram on damped-random-walk light curves matched to 12,400 bright, high-mass Palomar Transient Factory (PTF) quasars with Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 (DR7) masses. To test them over four decades of mass, we inject their sinusoidal and sawtooth signals into light curves of mergers in the TNG100-1 cosmological simulation, with magnitudes drawn from DR7 quasars of similar mass (extrapolated at low mass). We apply their threshold in each frequency bin, set by $10^5$ noise-only light curves per binary, on observed PTF cadences, one Stripe 82 cadence and an LSST-like cadence (Legacy Survey of Space and Time). At fixed absolute magnitude $M_i=-23$, sinusoid recovery falls toward high mass, and with DR7 magnitudes it climbs above about $10^8\,M_\odot$, so the magnitude assignment sets the sign of the trend. Above $10^8\,M_\odot$, where their sample lies, PTF sinusoid recovery is 39.8 against their 44.7 per cent. At LSST-like cadence sinusoid recovery is 76.9 per cent, about three times their 22.6 per cent, for reasons mostly unidentified. Denser sampling of the same PTF baselines did not lower recovery in any test. Even at LSST-like cadence we miss most sawtooth signals above $10^8\,M_\odot$. We tabulate recovery per 0.5-dex mass bin and cadence, with low-mass values likely too high for a deeper survey.
item.dc:creator: Karan Akbari, Sayantan Bhattacharya

item.title: Uncertainty estimation of incoming comet trajectories with a thermophysical non-gravitational force model for Comet Interceptor encounter planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.30871v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The European Space Agency Comet Interceptor mission is designed to fly-by an as-yet undetermined incoming long-period or dynamically-new comet, which will require an accurate prediction of its trajectory. Cometary orbits are perturbed from purely gravitational trajectories by non-gravitational accelerations (NGAs) stemming from their outgassing, however, and these must be taken into account in the navigation. We here test the ability of ground-based astrometry and standard NGA-fitting techniques to predict the position and velocity of incoming comets perturbed by a Monte Carlo sampled thermophysical acceleration model. We find that, due to the difficulties of predicting NGA evolution as well as the limitations of reasonably simulated astrometry, predicted accuracies are unlikely to meet the mission goals of 1000 km and 1 m s$^{-1}$ in position and velocity, sixty days before intercept. We instead recommend expanded uncertainties of $10,000$ km and several m s$^{-1}$. Our NGA fits struggle to reproduce the reference accelerations and trajectories when outgassing is rising steeply at a few AU-incoming, but with more observations up until perihelion, do eventually converge, leading to good estimates of many of the underlying acceleration parameters even for half an orbital arc.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Attree, Pieter de Boer, Pedro Guti\'errez, Pedro Lacerda, Michael K\"uppers, Dominic Dirkx

item.title: CURTAIN: Towards a Foundation Model for Neutrino Telescopes
item.description: arXiv:2610.30894v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neutrino telescopes record more than a trillion photon detections per year, yet there does not exist a self-supervised learning (SSL) task which fully satisfies all three conditions: improving as the pretraining set grows, transferring to a different detector, and outperforming the best model trained without pretraining at all. We introduce CURTAIN, a temporal masking scheme and the first SSL task for neutrino telescopes that achieves all of these goals. Downstream performance monotonically improves with the number of pretraining events, as predicted by scaling laws. Our encoder builds on DeepIce, currently the leading model on the NuBench benchmarks direction reconstruction task. Pretraining it with CURTAIN reduces its median angular error by 45% and its median energy error by 31% compared to training from scratch. It also transfers to a detector geometry never seen in pretraining, reducing the median angular error by 36% compared to training from scratch. At matched capacity and pretraining data, CURTAIN-pretrained encoders beat those pretrained by existing SSL tasks on both tasks and at every pretraining set size.
item.dc:creator: Severin Magel, Felix J. Yu, Carlos A. Arg\"uelles

item.title: Cross-Validation of Infrasound Detections and Fireball Observations from the Global Fireball Observatory
item.description: arXiv:2610.30936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How do infrasound signals from fireballs relate to atmospheric entry conditions and the physical properties of their parents meteoroids? In this study, we investigate the detectability of infrasound generated by local-to-regional fireballs and use the associated signals to constrain meteoroid physical properties. Across Western Australia and California, the Global Fireball Observatory (GFO) recorded nearly 300 fireball events with well-constrained trajectories within 500 km of an infrasound array over an 11-year period. Of these, 20 fireballs were confidently associated with infrasound detections. For these events, we estimate energies, constrain source altitudes using atmospheric ray-tracing simulations, and investigate source mechanisms using a multi-diagnostic approach. In particular, we examine whether the recorded infrasonic signals originated from cylindrical line sources (ballistic shocks) or discrete fragmentation episodes. Our results show that infrasound-detected fireballs span a broad range of dynamical and physical properties. This variability indicates that infrasound detectability is governed by a combination of source characteristics, atmospheric propagation conditions, and source-receiver geometry, rather than any single entry parameter. Analysis of the fireball shock source mechanisms reveals an even contribution from both ballistic and fragmentation-related sources. These results also demonstrate the value of combining infrasound and optical observations for robust constraints on meteoroid shock generation processes.
item.dc:creator: Iona Clemente, Eleanor K. Sansom, Hadrien A. R. Devillepoix, Elizabeth A. Silber, Svetlana B. Nikolova, Spiro Spiliopoulos, Peter Jenniskens, Jim Albers, Thomas Herring

item.title: Searching for substellar companion candidates with Gaia. V. M dwarfs within 15 pc studied with absolute astrometry, radial velocities, and direct imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.31006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we survey M-type stars within 15 pc observed by Gaia based on their colour, magnitude, and quality of astrometric data. We aim to detect new substellar companions using primarily Gaia astrometry and, when available, proper-motion anomaly (PMa) along with radial velocity (RV) and direct imaging (DI) data. We used the GaiaPMEX tool to search for bound companions around 582 M dwarfs. We identified all previously known stellar and planetary companions that were consistent with the Gaia excess signal. Then for all newly identified companions, we computed detection limits in the (mass, semi-major axis) parameter space using archival RV and DI data, to possibly rule out the presence of a stellar companion. The joint analysis of the parameter space allowed by astrometry and constrained by RV and DI provides tight constraints on the nature of the companion. We found 156 M dwarfs to have a bound companion within the Gaia sensitivity domain. The astrometric signals of 37 and seven of them are due to known stellar and substellar companions, respectively. We report 35 new substellar companions among which at least ten giant planets orbiting between 0.2 au and 2 au, with masses close to 1 M_Jup. We also report 77 substellar candidates, and provide detection limits using astrometry+RV+DI for 50 stars with known exoplanets and no significant Gaia excess noise. This work reveals a significant population of new substellar companions to M-type stars, challenging core accretion models. These results will be crucial inputs for estimating occurrence rates and studying the architecture of planetary systems around M dwarfs. Some new companions presented here, located beyond the water ice line, are prime targets for DI or coronagraphy observations with JWST or ELT.

item.title: A cosmic filament catalog for COSMOS-Web Data Release 1 across 0.5 < z < 3.5
item.description: arXiv:2610.31168v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cosmic filaments represent the environments in which most galaxies form and evolve. However, the spatial distribution of filaments and the link between galaxy properties and their positions relative to filaments remains unclear, particularly at high redshifts. In this work, using the deep-field catalog COSMOS-Web Data Release 1, we construct a filament catalog spanning 0.5 < z < 3.5 that can be directly applied to studies of galaxy evolution and the galaxy--large-scale-structure connection at the peak epoch of galaxy and black hole formation. We developed a new procedure based on the DisPerSE method that fully incorporates the probability distribution functions (PDFs) of galaxy photometric redshifts by generating multiple realizations for each tomographic 2D slice. We then stacked these realizations to construct ``filament probability maps'' (w_ fil maps), from which filaments were subsequently extracted. The filament extraction parameters were optimized using mock catalogs generated from TNG simulations by minimizing the discrepancies between 3D and projected 2D filaments. Applying this procedure to the COSMOS-Web data, we detected 12,523 filaments (comprising 136,210 segments) across 0.5 < z < 3.5 and released a filament catalog, a companion segment catalog, and filament probability maps for each slice. Validation against astrophysical properties shows a strong agreement between the extracted filaments and those in the simulations, supporting the robustness of the filament extraction. These data products provide a robust foundation for investigating galaxy--environment coevolution at cosmic noon and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Qiaoyang Hao, Tao Wang, Weishan Zhu, Hong Guo, Peng Wang, Tiancheng Yang, Luwenjia Zhou

item.title: The first selection of optimal targets for the Lazuli ExtraSolar Coronagraph's reflected starlight exoplanet campaign
item.description: arXiv:2610.31286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Direct detection and characterization of exoplanet atmospheres via reflected starlight enables probes of composition of mature exoplanet systems (since flux is decoupled from age) at closer separations than via thermal emission (due to observations in visible wavelengths), and even probes of biosignatures. New and upcoming ground and space-based platforms are enabling these observations for the first time. Recently the 3-m Lazuli Space Telescope, from the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Observatory System, was announced, which will be equipped with the ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC) designed for reflected light gas giant exoplanet observations in visible wavelengths. In this paper we present 27 known giant exoplanets that make up the first target list for these observations. Our target list spans ages and temperatures of planets not probed before by direct imaging, but some of which will also be accessible to the \textsl{Nancy Grace Roman} Coronagraph instrument and the ELT-METIS thermal imager, providing comprehensive atmosphere characterization and synergies. We discuss the science enabled by ESC observations of our target list and enhancements provided by future astrometric and radial velocity measurements.
item.dc:creator: Logan A. Pearce, Ewan Douglas

item.title: Multigroup Radiation Diffusion with Compton Scattering on a Moving Mesh: Implementation in RICH and Application to Tidal Disruption Events
item.description: arXiv:2610.31324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Compton scattering exchanges energy between radiation and hot gas and changes the spectrum in high-energy astrophysical systems such as tidal disruption events (TDEs). Because it couples all photon energies and can act faster than the hydrodynamic time step, many radiation-hydrodynamics (RHD) simulations omit its spectral redistribution or treat its energy exchange in the gray approximation. We extend the multigroup flux-limited diffusion module of the moving-mesh RHD code RICH to include Compton scattering with the exact thermal Compton kernel. In our semi-implicit scheme for the thermal radiative transfer equation, the temperature dependence of the kernel enters a generalized Fleck factor, and the group Compton operator conserves photon number and satisfies detailed balance. In equilibration tests, the scheme agrees with independent solutions, relaxes without absorption and emission to a Bose-Einstein spectrum, and remains stable for time steps that do not resolve the Compton equilibration timescale. We apply it to a three-dimensional simulation of the disruption of a $0.5\,M_\odot$ star by a $10^6\,M_\odot$ black hole. We find that during the X-ray flash, inverse Compton scattering dominates the coupling between the gas and the radiation near the nozzle shock, where it adds X-ray energy much faster than thermal emission and may affect the dynamics. Outside the X-ray thermalization radii, its instantaneous X-ray production rate during the flash is comparable to or larger than the escaping X-ray luminosity, so it may contribute substantially to the X-ray emission from TDEs.
item.dc:creator: Itamar Giron, Menahem Krief, Elad Steinberg

item.title: Hankel low-rank matrix approximation for gravitational-wave data analysis
item.description: arXiv:2603.15740v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) detectors, such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA), will observe vast numbers of overlapping signals. Disentangling these signals from instrumental noise and from one another constitutes a significant data analysis challenge. We explore a denoising technique based on embedding time series into Hankel matrices: a superposition of $n$ (damped) sinusoids corresponds to a matrix of rank $2n$. Thus, the problem of signal extraction is reduced to a structured low-rank approximation problem. Using synthetic data tailored to GW applications, we benchmark three Hankel-based algorithms: ESPRIT, Cadzow iterations, and iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS). Our test scenarios include isolated and multi-component monochromatic signals, the resolution of sources with closely spaced frequencies, and the recovery of black hole quasinormal modes (QNM). All three algorithms achieve near-optimal performance consistent with Fisher matrix bounds, evidenced by an inverse-square scaling of the mismatch with the signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, a proof-of-concept application to numerical relativity waveforms validates the ability of these algorithms to extract QNM frequencies from ringdown signals. Hankel low-rank approximation therefore offers a transparent, computationally efficient avenue for preprocessing GW time series.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Geissler, Vladimir Strokov, Christian K\"ummerle, Sergey Kushnarev, Emanuele Berti

item.title: Nested Sampling: A Critical and Comprehensive Theoretical Guide
item.description: arXiv:2606.17916v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The nested sampling (NS) technique has gained widespread attention, particularly in cosmology and astronomy, due to its ability to efficiently explore high-likelihood regions - a feature akin to an implicit likelihood optimization that underlies its success. While the full theoretical derivation of NS is complex and involves several approximations, the central challenge lies in sampling from the likelihood-constrained priors, which is crucial for its performance. This work provides a comprehensive and detailed exposition of NS derivation, clarifying both its theoretical foundations and practical challenges. We provide a thorough description of the NS procedure, emphasizing both its strengths and potential limitations. The connections between NS, importance sampling (IS), and vertical Monte Carlo are also discussed in detail. In doing so, this work seeks to deepen understanding of the method and to foster the development of future enhancements, novel variants, and more efficient implementations across a wide range of scientific applications. Thus, the main contribution of this work is twofold: it serves both as a tutorial for newcomers to the field and as a critical review for experienced practitioners.
item.dc:creator: Luca Martino, Fernando Llorente

item.title: Efficient Eccentric Effective-One-Body Dynamics via Near-Identity Averaging Transformations
item.description: arXiv:2606.30594v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Next-generation gravitational-wave detectors, such as LISA, the Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer, will require accurate and efficient models of long-lived black hole binary signals, including those with significant eccentricity. A challenge for eccentric effective-one-body models is the cost of resolving rapidly oscillating orbital dynamics over the inspiral, particularly for low-mass and large-mass-ratio systems. We address this by recasting the nonspinning eccentric effective-one-body equations of motion in terms of osculating orbital elements and then applying near-identity averaging transformations to eliminate the fast orbital-timescale structure during the inspiral. Each order in this procedure suppresses the oscillatory behavior by one factor of the ratio of orbital to radiation-reaction timescales. The resulting averaged dynamics are evolved on the radiation-reaction timescale, and then the system is mapped back to the full EOB dynamics for the final transition to plunge. This reduces the cost of the inspiral dynamics by up to two orders of magnitude, eliminating this as the primary bottleneck for long waveforms. The overall waveform-generation speedup spans $1.5 - 8 \times$, motivating the development of more efficient waveform-generation methods. We also validate the accuracy of the method by comparing waveforms generated from the averaged and full effective-one-body dynamics across a broad region of parameter space for moderate to large eccentricities. Carrying out this averaging procedure to next-to-next-to-leading order is needed to accurately model comparable-mass binaries, yielding mismatches $\leq 8.05 \times 10^{-5}$. These results establish near-identity averaging as a practical route to efficient eccentric effective-one-body inspirals, and provide a foundation for further extensions to low-eccentricity and spinning waveform models.
item.dc:creator: Philip Lynch, Alessandra Buonanno, Aldo Gamboa, Maarten van de Meent

item.title: Automated identification and subtraction of gravitational-wave glitches using boundary refinement
item.description: arXiv:2608.29295v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transient noise artifacts, or glitches, in gravitational wave strain data elevate the false alarm rate of astrophysical searches and degrade parameter estimation when overlapping a signal. No method previously identified a glitch's time boundary: existing detection and classification tools flag and label glitches without resolving their extent, forcing subtraction to run over padded windows that cost time and erase signal beyond the glitch itself. We present three boundary identification methods, AMPS (Amplitude-based Multi-glitch Pulse Segmenter), FLARE (Fitness-based Localization And Refinement Extractor), and CRISP (connected-region identification via spectrogram power), paired with three subtraction techniques, adaptive spline fitting, wavelet shrinkage, and their combination, across five glitches from the GravitySpy database spanning Advanced LIGO's first three observing runs. AMPS sets a boundary from a robust amplitude threshold, FLARE from the best fitness of a segmented spline fit, and CRISP from spectrogram power. Injecting a chirp signal on four broadband glitches, the combined technique recovers 95 to 97 percent of the injected signal-to-noise ratio, against roughly 64 percent for wavelet shrinkage alone. CRISP gives the most uniform boundary width across glitches; AMPS and CRISP both identify a boundary in a fraction of a second, two to three orders of magnitude faster than FLARE. For the glitch overlapping GW170817, a low-frequency residual persists under the default boundary, a deliberate tradeoff against removing signal power. Scattered light glitches remain untested and are the primary direction for future work.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Abu Thaher Chowdhury

item.title: Do Tabular Foundation Models Know Physics? Contamination, Units, and the Deterministic Limit
item.description: arXiv:2609.02766v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) learn to fill in tables the way language models fill in text --- and tables are arguably the format in which most physical measurement arrives. Did they learn any physics in the process? They are Bayesian by construction, so the question is what their prior contains. We probe it directly, evaluating four of them ($\texttt{TabPFN-3}$, $\texttt{TabICLv2}$, $\texttt{TabDPT}$ and $\texttt{Real-TabPFN-2.5}$) against six baselines on datasets sampled from 316 physical equations, in and out of domain. TFMs dominate, out of the box and after tuning. But they struggle to represent noiseless deterministic mechanisms in their uncertainty, and show no sign of exploiting physical units: they interpolate physics without yet being able to act as physical models.
item.dc:creator: Wassim Tenachi, Yashar Hezaveh, Laurence Perreault Levasseur, Pierre-Luc Bacon

item.title: simesh: A Python Framework for Quantitative Analysis of Native AMR Data from MPI-AMRVAC
item.description: arXiv:2610.29333v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) is widely used in large-scale astrophysical simulations, but the resulting multilevel data are challenging to analyze quantitatively. We present simesh, an independent Python framework for quantitative analysis of cell-centered fields on block-structured AMR meshes. The current implementation targets three-dimensional Cartesian datasets from MPI-AMRVAC and compatible AGILE snapshots, preserving the native AMR hierarchy and connecting complementary scientific diagnostics within a common numerical representation. The framework combines Python workflow interfaces with compiled Cython kernels, supporting efficient analysis on AMR meshes. We compare native AMR analysis with a VTK point-data conversion and uniform-grid resampling, which shows that changes in data association, interpolation support, and differentiation scale affect both sampled magnetic fields and derived current densities. Small differences in the sampled primary field can become more pronounced in derivative-based quantities, particularly near coarse-fine interfaces. The applications combine field diagnostics, tracing, regional statistics, and line-of-sight integration on the same native AMR representation. simesh makes these operations available through reusable Python interfaces for reproducible analysis of multiscale simulation data.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu, Jinhan Guo, Rony Keppens, Yang Guo
